name: Containers & Kubernetes
description: How containers actually work, writing good images, and the Kubernetes objects you cannot avoid.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Containers & Kubernetes is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is a container?
cards.answer: A lightweight, isolated package containing an application and everything it needs to run — code, runtime, libraries, configuration — that runs the same way on any machine with a container runtime.
cards.explanation: Containers solve "it works on my machine": the environment travels with the app. They share the host's operating-system kernel, which makes them start in seconds and use far less memory than virtual machines.

cards.prompt: Containers vs virtual machines
cards.answer: A virtual machine emulates a whole computer with its own operating system; a container isolates just an application, sharing the host's kernel.

left.title: Container
points: Starts in seconds, megabytes in size

right.title: Virtual machine
points: Starts in minutes, gigabytes in size

cards.explanation: They are often combined: cloud providers run your containers inside VMs, getting containers' efficiency with VMs' stronger isolation between customers.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between an image and a container?
cards.answer: An image is the read-only template — a packaged filesystem plus start-up instructions, built from a `Dockerfile`. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image. One image can run as many containers.
cards.explanation: Like a class and its objects. Images are stored and shared in registries such as Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry or a cloud provider's registry.

resources.title: Docker docs — What is an image?

cards.prompt: What do `docker build`, `docker run` and `docker ps` do?
cards.answer: `docker build -t myapp .` builds an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory. `docker run -p 8080:80 myapp` starts a container from it, mapping a host port to the container's port. `docker ps` lists running containers.
cards.explanation: Docker popularised containers in 2013; the formats are now open standards (OCI), so images built with Docker also run under Podman, containerd and Kubernetes.

cards.prompt: What is Kubernetes?
cards.answer: An open-source system for running containers across a cluster of machines: it schedules containers onto nodes, restarts them when they crash, scales them up and down, rolls out new versions and routes traffic to them.
cards.explanation: Kubernetes ("K8s") came out of Google in 2014 and is now the standard platform for running containers at scale. For a small app it is often overkill; simpler platforms run containers without the operational burden.

modules.name: Containers & Images
modules.description: Namespaces, cgroups, layers and building images that are small, fast and safe.

cards.prompt: Container vs virtual machine
cards.answer: A container is an isolated process on the host kernel (namespaces plus cgroups); a VM runs a full guest kernel on a hypervisor.

left.title: Container
points: Starts in milliseconds, megabytes of overhead
Weaker isolation boundary — kernel is shared
Linux containers need a Linux kernel

right.title: VM
points: Seconds to boot, gigabytes of overhead

cards.explanation: 'Containers are not a security boundary' is shorthand for: a kernel exploit escapes the container. That is why multi-tenant platforms use microVMs (Firecracker, gVisor). Docker on macOS and Windows runs a Linux VM underneath for the same reason.

resources.title: Docker docs — What is a container?

cards.prompt: Which kernel features make a container?
cards.answer: Namespaces provide isolation (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup) and cgroups enforce resource limits (CPU, memory, I/O, pids). Add a layered filesystem (overlayfs) plus capabilities, seccomp and MAC policies for the rest.
cards.explanation: There is no 'container' object in the kernel — it is a process with a particular set of namespaces and cgroups. That is why `ps` on the host shows container processes, and why a container OOM is really a cgroup memory limit being hit.

cards.prompt: Why does this Dockerfile reinstall every dependency on every code change?
cards.code:
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
cards.answer: `COPY . .` invalidates the cache whenever any file changes, so the `npm ci` layer is rebuilt every time. Copy the lockfiles first, install, then copy the source.
cards.explanation: Each instruction is a cached layer keyed on its inputs; once one is invalidated, every later layer rebuilds. Order from least to most frequently changing. A `.dockerignore` matters too — without it, `node_modules` and `.git` are shipped into the build context.

cards.prompt: What makes a production container image good?
cards.answer: Multi-stage build so no compilers ship, a minimal base (distroless, alpine or slim), a non-root USER, pinned base image digest, no secrets in layers, a healthcheck, and a small explicit set of files.
cards.explanation: Smaller images pull faster, start faster and have less to scan and patch. Remember that deleting a file in a later layer does not remove it from the image — a secret copied in layer 3 is still extractable even if layer 6 deletes it.

cards.prompt: Why should a container be stateless and treat its filesystem as ephemeral?
cards.answer: Because containers are recreated constantly — deploys, scaling, node failures, evictions. Anything written to the container filesystem disappears. State belongs in a database, an object store or a mounted volume.
cards.explanation: This is what makes horizontal scaling and zero-downtime deploys possible. The corollaries: configuration comes from the environment, logs go to stdout, and sessions live in a shared store rather than local memory.

modules.name: Kubernetes
modules.description: The objects, the control loop, and the operational realities.

cards.prompt: What do Pod, ReplicaSet, Deployment, Service and Ingress each do?
cards.answer: A Pod is one or more co-scheduled containers sharing a network namespace. A ReplicaSet keeps N pod copies running. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to give rolling updates and rollback. A Service gives a stable virtual IP and load balances to pods. An Ingress routes external HTTP traffic to Services.
cards.explanation: You almost never create Pods or ReplicaSets directly — you declare a Deployment and let the controllers converge. StatefulSets add stable identities and per-pod storage for databases; DaemonSets run one pod per node for agents.

cards.prompt: What is the reconciliation loop, and why is it the core idea of Kubernetes?
cards.answer: You declare desired state; controllers continuously observe actual state and act to close the gap. Nothing is a one-shot command — it is a loop that keeps running forever.
cards.explanation: This is why `kubectl apply` is idempotent, why deleting a pod recreates it, and why the same model extends to your own resources via CRDs and operators. It also means failures are usually 'the loop cannot converge' — read the events, not just the pod status.

cards.prompt: Liveness vs readiness vs startup probes
cards.answer: Liveness restarts a broken container; readiness removes a pod from Service endpoints; startup gives slow-booting apps time before the other probes apply.

right.title: Readiness
points: Failure → no traffic sent, pod kept
Fail it first during graceful shutdown

cards.explanation: The classic outage: a liveness probe that checks the database. The database blips, every pod fails liveness, the whole deployment restart-loops, and a minor dependency problem becomes a total outage.

resources.title: Kubernetes — Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes

cards.prompt: What is the difference between resource requests and limits, and what goes wrong with each?
cards.answer: Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits are the hard ceiling. Exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOM-killed; exceeding a CPU limit gets it throttled, not killed.
cards.explanation: CPU limits cause surprising latency: a bursty app is throttled every 100 ms period even when the node is idle. Common guidance is to set memory requests equal to limits and be cautious with CPU limits. No requests at all means BestEffort QoS — first to be evicted.

cards.prompt: When is Kubernetes the wrong choice?
cards.answer: When you have a handful of services, no dedicated platform capacity, and no need for its scheduling and self-healing. A managed container platform (ECS, Cloud Run, App Service, Fly) or plain VMs delivers faster with far less to learn and operate.
cards.explanation: Kubernetes is an excellent answer to problems of scale and heterogeneity: many teams, many services, bin-packing, portable primitives. Adopted too early it becomes the main thing the team maintains instead of the product.

modules.name: Docker in Depth
modules.description: ENTRYPOINT and CMD, tags and digests, volumes, networking, Compose, registries and scanning.

cards.prompt: Why does this container take 10 seconds to stop and drop in-flight requests?
cards.code:
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
CMD node server.js
cards.answer: The shell form (`CMD node server.js`) runs `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell is PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM to node; after the grace period the runtime sends SIGKILL. Use the exec form, `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`, so the app is PID 1 and receives signals — and handle SIGTERM in the app.
cards.explanation: `ENTRYPOINT` defines the executable; `CMD` supplies default arguments that `docker run image args` overrides. If a wrapper script is needed, end it with `exec "$@"`. Add `--init` (tini) when the process spawns children that must be reaped.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between an image tag and a digest?
cards.answer: A tag (`python:3.12-slim`, `myapp:latest`) is a mutable pointer that can be moved to a different image at any time. A digest (`@sha256:9f86…`) is the content hash of one exact image and can never change.
cards.explanation: Deploy by digest (or an immutable, unique tag such as the commit SHA) so what you tested is exactly what runs. Pin base images by digest too, and let a bot (Renovate, Dependabot) propose updates so you still receive security patches.

cards.prompt: Named volumes vs bind mounts
cards.answer: A named volume is storage managed by Docker, independent of the host's directory layout; a bind mount maps a specific host path into the container.

right.title: Bind mount
points: Depends on host layout and permissions
Can be slow on macOS and Windows

cards.explanation: Use volumes for persistent service data (a local Postgres) and bind mounts for development (live-editing source). Bind mounts expose host paths and permissions to the container — mounting the Docker socket or `/` into a container is effectively giving it root on the host.

cards.prompt: How do containers talk to each other and to the outside world?
cards.answer: On a user-defined bridge network, containers reach each other by container or service name through Docker's embedded DNS. Publishing a port (`-p 8080:80`) maps a host port to a container port for outside access. Inside a container, `localhost` means the container itself, not the host.
cards.explanation: The classic mistake is an app connecting to `localhost:5432` for a database in another container — use the service name (`db:5432`). Publish only what must be reachable, and bind to `127.0.0.1:` on the host for local-only services; published ports can bypass host firewall rules.

cards.prompt: What is Docker Compose for?
cards.answer: Defining and running a multi-container application from one YAML file — services, images or builds, environment, ports, volumes, networks and dependencies — so `docker compose up` starts the whole local stack: the app, its database, cache and any mocks.
cards.explanation: Compose is ideal for local development and integration tests; production usually runs on an orchestrator. `depends_on` only orders startup — add a healthcheck with `condition: service_healthy` so the app waits until the database actually accepts connections.

cards.prompt: A scanner reports 200 CVEs in your production image. What do you do first?
cards.answer: Shrink the attack surface — a minimal or distroless base removes most OS packages and their CVEs at once — then rebuild regularly on patched bases. Prioritise what remains by exploitability and reachability (known-exploited, network-facing, actually loaded) rather than by count.
cards.explanation: Scan in CI and in the registry continuously, since new CVEs appear for images that have not changed. Fail builds on fixable critical issues, not on every finding, or the gate gets disabled. Rebuilding weekly is often the single most effective control.

modules.name: Kubernetes in Practice
modules.description: Configuration and secrets, namespaces and RBAC, autoscaling, stateful workloads, disruptions, packaging, network policy and debugging.

cards.prompt: How do ConfigMaps and Secrets reach a pod, and why are Secrets not really secret by default?
cards.answer: Both are injected as environment variables or mounted files. Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted: anyone who can read them through the API, or read etcd without encryption at rest, sees the values.
cards.explanation: Enable etcd encryption at rest, restrict `get secrets` via RBAC, and prefer an external secret manager synchronised by the External Secrets Operator or a CSI driver. Mounted files update when the source changes; environment variables do not until the pod restarts.

resources.title: Kubernetes docs — Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets

cards.prompt: What do namespaces and RBAC provide in a Kubernetes cluster?
cards.answer: Namespaces partition resources by team or environment and scope names, quotas and policies. RBAC grants verbs (get, list, create…) on resources through Roles (namespaced) or ClusterRoles, bound to users, groups or service accounts.
cards.explanation: Namespaces are not a security boundary by themselves: without network policies, pods talk across them freely. Give every workload its own service account with the minimum permissions, and disable automounting API tokens for pods that never call the API.

cards.prompt: How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler work, and what does it depend on?
cards.answer: It periodically compares observed metrics — CPU or memory utilisation relative to *requests*, or custom and external metrics such as requests per second or queue depth — with a target, and adjusts the replica count between a minimum and a maximum.
cards.explanation: Without resource requests, utilisation-based scaling cannot work. Pair the HPA with a cluster autoscaler (or Karpenter) so new pods have nodes to land on, and use stabilisation windows to prevent flapping. KEDA scales on event sources, including down to zero.

cards.prompt: Deployment vs StatefulSet
cards.answer: Deployment pods are interchangeable — random names, shared or no storage, replaced in any order. StatefulSet pods have stable identities (`db-0`, `db-1`), stable DNS names, their own persistent volume each, and ordered start-up and termination.
cards.explanation: StatefulSets exist for clustered data stores that need identity and per-member storage. Even so, running databases on Kubernetes demands operators, backups and real expertise; a managed database is often the better choice.

cards.prompt: During node upgrades your three-replica service briefly goes fully down. What prevents that?
cards.answer: A PodDisruptionBudget (`minAvailable: 2`), which stops voluntary evictions such as node drains from taking too many pods at once. Also spread replicas across nodes and zones (topology spread constraints or anti-affinity), and tune the rolling update (`maxUnavailable: 0`, `maxSurge: 1`).
cards.explanation: PDBs only govern voluntary disruptions; they do not help if all replicas share one node that fails, which is what spreading addresses. Combined with readiness probes and graceful shutdown, these give zero-downtime deploys and maintenance.

resources.title: Kubernetes docs — Specifying a Disruption Budget

cards.prompt: Helm vs Kustomize
cards.answer: Helm packages manifests as charts with Go templates and a values file, with releases, versioning and rollback. Kustomize layers plain YAML with patches and overlays per environment, with no templating language.
cards.explanation: Helm suits distributing reusable software (most third-party installs are charts); Kustomize suits your own services where overlays for dev, staging and prod are enough. Heavy template logic in charts becomes hard to review — keep values simple and render the output in CI to diff it.

cards.prompt: What is a NetworkPolicy, and what is the default without one?
cards.answer: Without any policy, every pod can reach every other pod in the cluster. A NetworkPolicy selects pods and allows specific ingress and egress (from certain pods, namespaces or IP ranges, on certain ports); once a pod is selected, everything else is denied.
cards.explanation: Start with a default-deny policy per namespace and allow flows explicitly — it contains lateral movement from a compromised pod. Enforcement needs a CNI plugin that supports it (Calico, Cilium); on one that does not, policies are silently ignored.

cards.prompt: A pod is stuck in `CrashLoopBackOff`. How do you investigate?
cards.answer: `kubectl describe pod` for events, exit codes and the reason (OOMKilled, failed probe, image pull error); `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` for the crashed container's last output; then `kubectl debug` or `exec` into a running copy to inspect config, environment and connectivity.
cards.explanation: Common causes: missing config or secrets, the app exiting immediately (wrong command), a liveness probe killing a slow-starting app (use a startup probe), OOM from a tight memory limit, or a dependency that is unreachable. Events usually point the way within a minute.
